title: Expanding brackets
examples: When do I need to use the FOIL method?
Is there a pattern I should remember for expanding?
What if one of the brackets has a negative sign?

explain.say: Today we are learning to expand brackets. This means multiplying the brackets out. We will start with single brackets first. Remember to multiply the outside term by every term inside.

items: Multiply outside term by every inside term

explain.say: For example, look at x times the bracket of two plus three. You multiply x by two, and then you multiply x by three. The answer is two x squared plus three x.

items: Multiply x by 2, then x by 3

explain.say: Next we move to double brackets. This means we have two sets of brackets to multiply. We must multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second bracket.

items: Multiply first bracket by every term in second

explain.say: We can use the FOIL method for this. F stands for first, O for outer, I for inner, and L for last. Let us try x plus three times x minus five. First is x times x, outer is x times minus five, inner is three times x, and last is three times minus five. This gives x squared minus five x plus three x minus fifteen.
Finally, we can simplify the result. We combine the like terms in the middle. The five x and three x become minus two x. So the final answer is x squared minus two x minus fifteen.

faq.q: What is the difference between expanding and simplifying?
faq.a: Expanding means multiplying the brackets out completely. Simplifying means combining any like terms you find after expanding. You do both steps when you are done.
asks: Do I always have to simplify?
What does it mean to simplify an expression?

faq.q: Does the FOIL method only work for two brackets?
faq.a: The FOIL method is a helpful way to remember the process for two brackets. When you have more, you must multiply every term by every other term.
asks: How do I expand three brackets?
Is FOIL just a trick for two brackets?

faq.q: What if I have three brackets to multiply?
faq.a: You must multiply the first two brackets together first. Then you take that entire result and multiply it by the third bracket. You work step by step.
asks: What is the order for three brackets?

faq.q: Do I need to use brackets when I multiply?
faq.a: Yes, using brackets helps keep your terms organised. They show you which parts of the expression must be multiplied together. It keeps your work neat.
asks: Why are brackets important in algebra?

faq.q: What is the rule for multiplying negative numbers?
faq.a: Remember that a negative times a negative equals a positive. A negative times a positive is always negative. This is important for the last step.
asks: What is the sign rule for multiplication?

facts: Multiplying a single bracket means distributing the outside term.
When expanding two brackets, every term must meet every other term.
The FOIL method stands for First, Outer, Inner, Last.
The product of two binomials always results in a quadratic expression.

quiz.why: You multiply four by x, and then you multiply four by two. This gives four x plus eight.

wrong.0: This mistake only multiplies the first terms and ignores the second term.
wrong.1: This mistake incorrectly multiplies the two numbers together.
wrong.2: This mistake adds the numbers instead of multiplying them.

quiz.why: Using FOIL, you get x times x, x times three, one times x, and one times three. Combining the middle terms gives four x.

wrong.0: This mistake only uses the first and last terms from the expansion.
wrong.1: This mistake forgets to multiply the constant terms together.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly uses the first term from the second bracket.

quiz.why: First is two x times x, outer is two x times plus two, inner is minus three times x, and last is minus three times plus two. Combining gives the result.

wrong.1: This mistake adds the outer and inner terms incorrectly.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly calculates the last term's sign.
wrong.3: This mistake ignores the multiplication of the last two terms.
